study.title: Finding a Partner
study.question: Who in our community cares for the environment, and how can we help?
study.passage:
Partner research (written for this lesson):
Types of partners: your municipality's parks or environment department; local stewardship or "friends of" park groups; watershed councils (Alberta has Watershed Planning and Advisory Councils for major basins); naturalist clubs; Indigenous organizations; land trusts; school district sustainability staff.
Research (20 minutes): in groups, find two possible partners. Record: name, mission, projects, how they work with youth, contact info (from official websites).
Choose: which partner best fits the class's interests and the schoolyard or community needs identified earlier?
Professional email (teacher sends from the school account): greeting; who we are (grade 8 Outdoor Ed class, school name); what we've learned; what we hope to do together; dates that work; thanks and closing. Keep it short and specific.
Partnership qualities: shared goals, clear roles, good communication, mutual benefit (students learn and help; the group gets volunteers and youth engagement), respect for the partner's expertise.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; organization types are general examples.
steps: Discuss qualities of a good partnership

study.title: Planning a Restoration
study.question: How do we plan a restoration project that helps habitat recover?
study.passage:
Restoration planning (written for this lesson):
Alberta's Weed Control Act classifies some invasive plants as "prohibited noxious" (must be destroyed) or "noxious" (must be controlled). Examples: purple loosestrife, garlic mustard (prohibited noxious); Canada thistle, oxeye daisy, common tansy, leafy spurge (noxious).
Native alternatives: willows and red-osier dogwood along streams; prairie crocus, wild bergamot, fireweed, goldenrod and native grasses in open areas.
Plan with your partner: 1. Site: where will we work? Walk it with the partner. 2. Activity: pulling invasive weeds, planting native seedlings, live-staking willows, litter clean-up, building a fence to keep people off a recovering area. 3. Identify: learn to recognize the target invasive plant and look-alikes (with partner guidance). 4. Logistics: date, transport, permission forms, gloves, tools, bags for weeds (bag invasive seeds; don't compost), water, first aid, washrooms. 5. Safety: wear gloves (some plants irritate skin); no tool use without instruction. 6. Measures: count plants pulled or planted, area restored, before/after photos.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; plant classifications from Alberta's Weed Control Regulation.

study.title: Restore, Evaluate, Share
study.question: How do we carry out and evaluate a restoration project?
study.passage:
Restoration day and evaluation (written for this lesson):
1. Arrival and briefing: partner explains the site, target plants, tools and safety.
2. Work in teams: record counts (plants pulled or planted, bags filled, area covered); take before/after photos from the same spots ("photo points").
3. Wrap-up circle: one thing learned, one thing noticed about the land.
4. Evaluation (back at school): compare outcomes with your goals: e.g. "Goal: 200 native seedlings planted; outcome: 230." Survey participants and the partner: what worked, what to improve?
5. Impact report (one page): goals, what we did, numbers, photos, quotes, lessons learned, next steps.
6. Gratitude: send thank-you notes or a short video to the partner.
7. Share: post the impact report on the school website or newsletter with permission.
8. Follow-up monitoring: plan a return visit (e.g. in spring) to check seedling survival or weed regrowth at the same photo points.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
